issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the study as using a national probability/general population sample, but the Methods state that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool and were predominantly young students. This is a fundamental contradiction that changes the population, sampling frame, design, and interpretation of every result.
issues.quote: "We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years." / "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington."

issues.description: The Discussion and Conclusion claim national representativeness and high generalisability, but the reported sample is small, young, mostly female, and mostly Pākehā psychology-pool participants. These claims are not supported by the described sampling procedure or demographics.
issues.quote: "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population."

issues.description: Recruitment from an introductory psychology participant pool creates a convenience/student sample, not a probability sample of the general population. The sample composition also suggests strong selection bias and limited representativeness, undermining claims about the general population.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European)."

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistent with reported precision
issues.description: The reported confidence intervals and p-values are far too precise for N = 374. For example, r = -.08 with N = 374 would not yield p < .001 and the CIs for means/correlations would be much wider. This suggests either the sample size is wrong, the table was computed from a different dataset, or the statistics are misreported.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study" / "WILL | -.25*** [-.27, -.22] | -.08*** [-.11, -.05] | .76"

issues.subcategory: impossible RMSEA given chi-square, df, and N
issues.description: Given N = 374, χ2 = 36511.73, and df = 2279, the RMSEA would be approximately .20, not .03. The reported fit indices are mathematically inconsistent with the reported sample size and chi-square, indicating a serious reporting or analytic error.

issues.subcategory: model fit accepted despite poor fit
issues.description: The model is accepted despite a very poor chi-square test and CFI = .86, which is below conventional thresholds for acceptable fit. The authors selectively emphasize RMSEA and SRMR while dismissing contradictory evidence of poor model fit, which undermines confidence in the structural estimates.
issues.quote: "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted."

issues.subcategory: confidence interval does not match rounded RMSEA
issues.description: The reported RMSEA estimate is .03, but the 90% confidence interval is [.025, .026]. Although rounding may partly explain this, the point estimate should fall within the confidence interval on the reported scale or be reported with adequate precision. As written, the estimate and interval appear inconsistent.

issues.subcategory: model described as path analysis but item-level residual constraints reported
issues.description: The analysis is described as a path analysis with three variables across five time points, but the authors also refer to constraining item residual variances over time. A path model of three observed composites would not have item residual variances. This creates ambiguity about whether the analysis was a manifest-variable path model or a latent-variable SEM, and prevents evaluation or replication.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points" / "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.description: Key SEM details are missing: whether constructs were modeled as latent or observed, estimator, treatment of ordinal Likert items, factor loadings, residual covariances, intercept constraints, within-wave covariances, equality constraints, and whether robust/scaled chi-square difference tests were used. Without these details the model cannot be evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29])."

issues.description: The manuscript alternates among environmentalism, environmental concern, willingness to change behavior, and willingness to sacrifice as if they are the same construct. The actual items measure concern and perceived exaggeration, not willingness to sacrifice or behavior change. This undermines construct validity and makes the substantive conclusions about behavioral willingness unsupported.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems" / "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment."

issues.subcategory: measure does not assess willingness to sacrifice
issues.description: The variable labeled WILL is interpreted as willingness to make sacrifices for the environment, but the two quoted items ask about concern and whether environmental problems are exaggerated. Neither item directly measures willingness to sacrifice, behavioral intention, or actual behavior.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, ‘How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?’ and ‘To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?’"

issues.subcategory: environmentalism conflated with climate change attitudes
issues.description: The Introduction and Discussion frame the study around climate change denial and climate change mitigation, but the outcome measure asks about the natural environment generally and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. General environmental concern is not equivalent to climate change denial, climate mitigation behavior, or willingness to act on climate change.
issues.quote: "Research on the psychological foundations of climate change denial have highlighted the important role of two ideological attitudes" / "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems."

issues.description: The authors infer that high-SDO participants have a motivation to exploit the environment, but exploitation motives were not measured. Lower concern or lower stated willingness to sacrifice cannot establish a motive to exploit nature or other groups.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance"

issues.description: The manuscript interprets the RWA effect as reflecting a desire to submit to authority/tradition, but the short RWA scale includes multiple components and the study does not isolate submission, aggression, or conventionalism. This is especially problematic because the Introduction itself notes that RWA dimensions may relate differently to environmentalism.
issues.quote: "the desire to submit to tradition and authority" / "Reese [20] found that the dimensions of RWA differentially predict pro-environmental attitudes: authoritarian submission predicts greater pro-environmentalism, authoritarian aggression predicts lower pro-environmentalism, whilst the preference for tradition is unrelated."

issues.description: One RWA item was omitted at Time 2 but included at all other waves. This changes the content and reliability of the RWA scale over time and threatens longitudinal comparability unless explicitly modeled and tested. The manuscript does not explain how this missing item was handled in scoring or SEM.
issues.quote: "The item ‘Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done’, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.description: The study makes longitudinal claims about changes in SDO, RWA, and environmentalism, but does not report tests of measurement invariance across the five waves. This is especially important because short scales were used and one RWA item was absent at Time 2. Without invariance, cross-lagged paths may reflect changes in measurement rather than changes in constructs.
issues.quote: "Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items" / "Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with six items" / "The item ... was not assessed at time two"

issues.subcategory: scale scoring and reverse coding unclear
issues.description: The manuscript does not state how equality-favoring SDO items, the reverse-worded RWA item, or the environmental exaggeration item were reverse coded or combined. This omission impedes replication and could affect the sign and interpretation of associations.
issues.quote: "Three items favoured dominance ... and three favoured equality" / "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.description: Reliabilities appear on the diagonal of Table 1 but are not labeled as alpha, omega, or another coefficient, and only Time 1 reliabilities are reported. For longitudinal analyses, reliabilities at every wave are needed, especially given short scales and a missing RWA item at Time 2.
issues.quote: "Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used"

issues.description: Listwise deletion across five waves can substantially reduce power and bias estimates unless data are missing completely at random. The manuscript provides no missingness diagnostics, no attrition analysis, and no justification for not using FIML or multiple imputation.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.description: The study spans five measurement points, yet the manuscript does not report initial N, wave-specific Ns, dropout rates, reasons for attrition, or whether retained participants differed from dropouts. Referring readers to a website is insufficient for peer review and replication.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: The wording implies that only participants who participated across all five semesters/waves were included. Restricting analyses to complete cases can produce a select, more compliant subset and bias longitudinal estimates, especially if ideological or environmental attitudes predict continued participation.
issues.quote: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project"

issues.description: The manuscript describes the design as five years/five time points, but the Methods say participants participated across five semesters. Five semesters is not equivalent to five years, and the timing of waves is unclear.
issues.quote: "over five years" / "participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)"

issues.description: Cross-lagged models depend on the interval between measurements. The manuscript does not clearly state whether the five waves were annual, semester-based, or irregular, nor whether all lags were equal. This is important because stationarity constraints assume comparable lag intervals.
issues.quote: "participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)"

issues.description: The authors impose equality constraints on cross-lagged parameters across all lags because of their substantive interest, not because they demonstrate that stationarity fits as well as a less constrained model. If effects vary over time, the imposed constraints can bias estimates and obscure developmental or contextual changes.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states twice that cross-lagged associations were constrained to be equal across measurement points, suggesting editing errors and creating uncertainty about exactly which constraints were applied.
issues.quote: "We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point." / "Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point."

issues.description: The authors justify p < .05 by citing a large sample size, but larger samples make trivial effects statistically significant and generally increase the need to emphasize effect sizes, precision, and practical significance. The statement is also inconsistent with the reported N = 374, which is not especially large for a complex five-wave SEM.
issues.quote: "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings."

issues.description: The Methods specify p < .05 as the significance threshold, while the figure caption says all parameters meet p < .01 unless otherwise noted. The manuscript does not explain which threshold governs inference.
issues.quote: "we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05" / "All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted."

issues.subcategory: SDO stronger claim contradicted by test
issues.description: The authors directly test whether the SDO and RWA paths differ and obtain p = .126, which is not statistically significant. They nevertheless interpret SDO as the stronger predictor. This is a serious inferential error, repeated in the Discussion as a significant difference.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor"

issues.subcategory: unsupported statement that SDO is significantly stronger
issues.description: The Discussion says SDO is significantly stronger than RWA, but the reported equality test for the SDO and RWA paths was non-significant. This overstates the evidence and misrepresents the statistical result.
issues.quote: "In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.description: The authors base claims about comparative predictive strength on unstandardized coefficients. Even when predictors have similar response ranges, their variances and reliabilities differ, and reciprocal paths have different outcomes. Comparisons of effect magnitude require standardized estimates or properly specified equality tests on commensurate scales.
issues.quote: "based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor"

issues.subcategory: Wald test claim incorrect or unexplained
issues.description: The authors state that a traditional Wald test is not possible because of constraints, but SEM software such as Mplus can usually test equality constraints using MODEL TEST or nested model comparisons. The manuscript does not explain why a Wald test is impossible, raising concern about the comparison procedure.
issues.quote: "Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible."

issues.subcategory: coefficient, SE, CI, and p-value inconsistencies
issues.description: The manuscript reports uncertainty as SD rather than SE, and some p-values appear inconsistent with the coefficient and reported uncertainty. For example, B = -.02 with SD/SE = .01 would not normally yield p = .001 unless the rounded values hide substantial precision. This should be clarified and corrected.

issues.subcategory: standard errors mislabeled as standard deviations
issues.description: The reported quantities accompanying regression/path coefficients are labeled SD, but for hypothesis tests and confidence intervals these should be standard errors. Mislabeling uncertainty estimates impairs interpretation and suggests possible reporting confusion.

The text says the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse, but the reported unstandardized coefficients show environmentalism to SDO as B = -.04 and SDO to environmentalism as B = -.11. The following sentence then says SDO has the stronger influence. The direction of the claimed stronger effect is internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: "The lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on both SDO and RWA were statistically significant" / "the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse" / "suggest that SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse."

issues.description: The reported difference test for the SDO-RWA reciprocal paths is enormous, χ2(1) = 15,389.13, despite the reported paths being B = .02 and B = -.001. This value is implausible for the reported N = 374 and suggests a transcription, scaling, or analytic error.
issues.quote: "Whilst the lagged effect of RWA on SDO was statistically significant (B = .02, SD = .003, p < .001, 95% CI [.02, .03]), SDO did not predict change in RWA (B = -.001, SD = .01, p = .859, 95% CI [-.01, .01]). These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.subcategory: dependent correlations compared by CI overlap
issues.description: The authors infer that one zero-order correlation is stronger than another because confidence intervals do not overlap. Correlations sharing a variable should be compared with a formal test for dependent correlations; CI non-overlap is conservative and not the appropriate inferential method.
issues.quote: "the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.subcategory: causal claims from observational cross-lagged data
issues.description: The study is observational and survey-based. Cross-lagged paths can provide temporal ordering but do not establish causality, especially without randomization, manipulation, or strong controls for time-varying and stable confounds. The manuscript repeatedly makes causal claims that are not justified.
issues.quote: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism."

issues.description: The analyses do not appear to control for plausible confounds such as political orientation, socioeconomic status, education, ethnicity, gender, age, religiosity, personality, or cohort effects. These variables may influence both ideological attitudes and environmental concern, so cross-lagged associations cannot be interpreted causally.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points"

issues.subcategory: authors acknowledge third-variable explanation but do not address it analytically
issues.description: The Discussion acknowledges that a third variable could explain the bidirectional associations, but this possibility is not incorporated into the analyses. Acknowledgment after the fact does not resolve the causal identification problem.
issues.quote: "Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable."

issues.subcategory: traditional CLPM conflates within- and between-person effects
issues.description: The use of a standard cross-lagged panel model does not separate stable between-person differences from within-person change. Therefore, the reported cross-lagged paths may reflect trait-like between-person associations rather than within-person causal influence over time. A random-intercept CLPM or related approach would be needed to support within-person change claims.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model"

issues.description: The manuscript uses language such as 'leads to' and 'influence' to describe nonexperimental associations. This overstates what the design can support.
issues.quote: "The preference for an unequal society leads individuals to be less willing to make personal sacrifices for the environment."

issues.description: The conclusion that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance is not measured or identified by the model. A cross-lagged association between RWA and SDO cannot establish socialization processes or their relative strength.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."

issues.subcategory: overextension from New Zealand student data to broad climate communication recommendations
issues.description: The manuscript recommends targeting high-SDO individuals in climate change communication, but the reported sample is narrow and the measured outcome is not climate action. The generalization from a New Zealand psychology-pool sample and two-item environmental concern measure to communication strategy is premature.
issues.quote: "Our findings highlight endorsers of SDO as targets for climate change communications."

issues.subcategory: survey weights and complex sampling not reported
issues.description: If the study truly used a national probability/NZAVS sample, analyses should report whether sampling weights, stratification, clustering, and post-stratification adjustments were used. If it used a student participant pool, probability-sample claims should be removed. The current manuscript gives no basis for evaluating design-based inference.
issues.quote: "national probability sample" / "conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29])"

issues.description: The authors state that Mplus syntax will be available only upon acceptance, which prevents reviewers from verifying model specification, constraints, estimator choices, handling of missing data, and tests. For a complex and internally inconsistent SEM, withholding syntax until acceptance weakens transparency.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.description: The manuscript does not report preregistration or an a priori analysis plan. Given multiple possible operationalizations of environmentalism, alternative lag structures, stationarity constraints, missing-data approaches, and model specifications, undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom are a concern.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects"

issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics and correlations are reported. For a five-wave longitudinal study, readers need wave-specific means, variances, reliabilities, sample sizes, missingness, and cross-wave correlations to evaluate stability, attrition, stationarity, and measurement quality.
issues.quote: "Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1."

issues.description: The manuscript does not report ethics approval, informed consent procedures, or participant compensation/credit, despite using longitudinal human-subjects data from students or NZAVS participants. These details are needed to evaluate ethical conduct and sampling incentives.
issues.quote: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington."

issues.subcategory: external website substituted for core methods
issues.description: Critical methodological details are deferred to the NZAVS website rather than included in the manuscript. Peer reviewers and readers need enough information in the article itself to evaluate recruitment, retention, inclusion criteria, and procedure.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: The Acknowledgments thank the NZAVS team for data collection, while the Methods state that participants were recruited through a Victoria University introductory psychology pool. This reinforces uncertainty about which dataset was actually analyzed.
issues.quote: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." / "We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team for their work collecting and maintaining the NZAVS."

issues.description: The study uses self-report attitude items but draws conclusions about willingness to behave pro-environmentally and environmental action. Attitudes, intentions, and behavior are distinct constructs; without behavioral measures, conclusions about action or behavior change are unsupported.
issues.quote: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment" / "participants’ concern about environmental problems"

issues.subcategory: no control for mode or cohort/context effects
issues.description: The study spans 2009–2013, a period during which public discourse, economic conditions, environmental events, or political changes could affect both ideology and environmental attitudes. The model does not report controls for period effects or contextual shocks.

issues.subcategory: multiple testing and practical significance not addressed
issues.description: The manuscript emphasizes statistical significance for many paths but does not discuss multiplicity, effect sizes, or practical importance. Some reported effects are very small, such as B = -.01 or B = -.02, yet are interpreted substantively.

issues.subcategory: environment as an outgroup asserted without direct test
issues.description: The manuscript theorizes that nature may function as an outgroup for high-SDO individuals, but the study does not measure perceptions of nature as an outgroup, human-nature dominance, environmental hierarchy, or resource-based intergroup competition. The theoretical mechanism is therefore not tested.
issues.quote: "This is perhaps the first hint that for those endorsing SDO, nature might be another ‘outgroup’ to assert dominance over."

issues.subcategory: mechanism claims unsupported by measured variables
issues.description: The Discussion develops a mechanism involving environmental inequality and dominance over low-status groups, but the study measures only SDO, RWA, and a two-item environmental attitude variable. No measures of perceived inequality, environmental justice, group threat, or distribution of environmental harms are included.
issues.quote: "Exploitation of natural resources favours the dominant group, while the consequences fall to those at the bottom of the hierarchy."
